To expound means to explain something in a thorough, detailed, and careful way — usually an idea, theory, belief, or philosophy — so that the listener or reader truly understands it at a deep level.

It is not a quick, surface-level explanation. When someone expounds something, they are unfolding it, layer by layer, so all its parts, implications, and meaning become clear.
What Makes It Different From Just "Explain"

The word "explain" is broad and everyday. You can explain how to tie your shoes. But you would not normally use "expound" for something so simple or practical.

Expound carries extra weight. It suggests:

  • The subject matter is complex, abstract, or intellectual — a philosophy, a theory, a belief system, a doctrine, a viewpoint.
  • The person doing the expounding has knowledge, authority, or deep familiarity with the subject.
  • The explanation is systematic and thorough, not rushed or casual.

Think of a professor spending an entire lecture carefully walking students through Einstein's theory of relativity — that is expounding. A friend quickly telling you what the theory is about — that is explaining.
The Two Ways It Is Used

1. Expound something (without "on")

Here, you expound the thing directly. You lay it out, present it fully.

  • The philosopher expounded his theory of consciousness.
  • She expounded her views on climate policy in a 40-page report.
  • The preacher expounded the scripture for an hour.

2. Expound on (or upon) something

Here, you go deeper into a topic that has already been mentioned or introduced. This version is extremely common in everyday formal speech and writing.

  • The professor asked the student to expound on her answer.
  • The scientist expounded on the dangers of the new virus.
  • Could you expound on what you mean by "freedom"?

Both usages mean essentially the same thing — the "on/upon" version just places a slight emphasis on elaborating further on something already on the table.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Expound is a formal word. It lives in the world of lectures, academic writing, religious sermons, philosophical debate, journalism, and formal speeches. You would not hear it in casual conversation very often. If someone at a dinner party says, "Let me expound on why I love this pasta," it would sound oddly stiff — almost comic. But in a documentary, a courtroom, or an essay, it fits perfectly.

The word also carries a quiet sense of authority and seriousness. When you say someone expounded an idea, you are implying they knew it well and presented it with care and depth — not that they were just guessing or skimming the surface.

The subject of expounding is almost always something abstract or conceptual. Common examples:

  • A theory (scientific, philosophical, economic)
  • A belief or religious doctrine
  • A political view or ideology
  • A plan or vision
  • A piece of literature or text (especially religious scripture)
  • A personal philosophy

You expound ideas. You do not expound a chair, a meal, or a route on a map.

• He was asked to expound on his earlier statement.
  • The teacher expounded the rules of grammar with great patience.
  • Darwin expounded his theory of evolution in "On the Origin of Species."
  • The lawyer expounded upon the legal precedents that supported her argument.
  • The guru spent years expounding the principles of mindfulness to his students.

Think of it this way: to expound is to open something up completely — like unfolding a map so every road, every detail, every corner is visible. You are not just pointing at the map. You are spreading it out, reading it aloud, and making sure everyone around you understands every part of it.
